subject: ventures/depreciation-recapture-calculator
professional: a CPA who prepares Form 4797 and the Schedule D Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet for landlords and handles Section 1031 boot; first checks: is basis reduced by depreciation allowed or allowable (not only claimed), is Section 1245 property (cost-segregation components, appliances, bonus) recaptured as fully ordinary income rather than at the 25% rate, is the 25% gain capped at the gain and taxed at no more than the seller's ordinary rate per section 1(h)(1)(E), is recognized boot limited to the realized gain under section 1031(b), and does the capital-gains rate respond to how large the gain is

evidence.correctness: Ran the shipped page in Chromium (Playwright, python3 -m http.server) and recomputed by hand from Pub 544 ch. 4 (gain = amount realized - adjusted basis; adjusted basis reduced by depreciation), the Schedule D Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet and IRC 1(h)(1)(E) (25% max rate), and IRC 1031(b) (gain recognized = lesser of boot or realized gain). Example: basis 300,000+20,000-87,000 = 233,000, realized 395,000, gain 162,000, 87,000 x 25% = 21,750, 75,000 x 15% = 11,250, total 33,000: page shows the same. Boot page example (200k/100k dep/500k-30k, boot 50k): 12,500 due, 53,000 deferred; matches. NIIT + 120k boot: 21,750 + 4,950 + 4,560 = 31,260 due, 7,896 deferred; matches. Ordinary rate 22: 19,140; matches. The engine is right for its model, but the UI path for the ordinary-rate override is mislabelled '($, optional)' and silently reads 0.22 as 0.22%: recapture tax $191.40 instead of $19,140 with no warning (observed in Chromium). Basis uses only depreciation 'claimed', not 'allowed or allowable' (Pub 544), and all depreciation is taxed at the 25% cap even when part is Section 1245 property (cost seg, which the page footer links to), where Form 4797 Part III recaptures it as ordinary income up to 37%. A reachable silent wrong number plus unflagged rule departures caps this at 2.
evidence.completeness: README and llms.txt claim: adjusted basis/gain, 1250 split, LTCG rate, optional NIIT, 1031 boot tax and deferral, findings for each simplification, shareable link, local-only usage counts, opt-out. All worked end to end in Chromium (example, shared-link prefill from the boot page, NIIT, boot, loss case); no console errors; no horizontal scroll at 375 px. Gaps: the loss case prints 'the entire -$60,000.00 gain ... would be deferred'; land value has no effect on any output (changing it 60,000 -> 0 left every figure unchanged).
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs' in the subject root: 50 tests, 50 pass. Tests include a hand-computed worked example and boot tests. Three seeded mutations via quality_mutate.py: recaptureRate min->max caught; exchange LTCG at recapture rate caught; NIIT on boot computed on the whole gain instead of the recognized gain SURVIVED (no test combines includeNiit with boot). No test checks the ordinary-rate field's label/units or the page's percent-to-decimal conversion (index.html:195), which is where the high defect lives.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs, share.mjs, usage.mjs, index.html and the three content pages. Small pure modules, one shared splitGain for sale and boot paths, share field list derived from DEFAULTS, storage access wrapped. Defects: depreciableBasis computed and returned but never used or shown (calc.mjs:128); no validation that depreciation taken <= purchasePrice - landValue + improvements; num() silently turns bad input into 0; findings rendered by innerHTML (static strings, no injection today).
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, no-warranty, privacy, not-affiliated and no-price-for-Realized claims are present and backed (vs-realized1031.test.mjs). served-copy.mjs reports no placeholder or retired origin in llms.txt/sitemap/robots/canonicals. Unbacked or wrong: the ordinary-rate label says '($, optional)' for a percentage (index.html:80); index.html:147 says it applies 'standard capital-gains brackets' but it applies one user-picked flat rate; README says findings disclose 'every simplification', yet Section 1245 recapture, allowed-or-allowable, bracket stacking and the 1231 look-back are not flagged; vs-doing-it-by-hand.html:44 says it 'keeps land value out of the depreciable basis', but land value changes no output and depreciation is never checked against the depreciable basis. Comparison-page arithmetic (17.70% blended, $8,851 vs $12,500, crossover table) recomputed and correct.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job of a landlord with a straight-line-only residential rental who knows their total depreciation and marginal rate: they get a correct planning split and boot estimate in a minute, and can send a link to their CPA. A landlord who did a cost-segregation study or bonus depreciation, who never claimed depreciation, whose gain crosses the 15%/20% or 0%/15% threshold, or who types a decimal rate gets a wrong number with no flag. A CPA would use it only as a back-of-envelope.
evidence.domain: Compared with Pub 544 ch. 3-4, Form 4797 instructions (Part III, lines 22-29: 1245 vs 1250), the Schedule D Tax Worksheet and IRC 1(h), 1411, 1031. Matches: 25% max rate on unrecaptured 1250 gain, cap at the lesser of depreciation or gain, recapture-first ordering on recognized boot, 1031(b) gain limit, 45/180-day rule, NIIT 3.8% with $200k/$250k untindexed thresholds (flagged as simplified). Departs: no 'allowed or allowable' basis rule; no Section 1245 ordinary recapture; min(marginal, 25%) instead of the worksheet's bracket stacking; flat LTCG rate with no income stacking; loss finding misstates the 1231(c) look-back (it recharacterizes later gains, it does not limit this loss).

defects.what: The ordinary-marginal-rate override is labelled '($, optional)' and divides the entry by 100 with no range check: a seller who types 0.22 for 22% gets a recapture tax of $191.40 instead of $19,140 on the example, with no warning.

All depreciation is taxed as unrecaptured 1250 gain at up to 25%; depreciation on Section 1245 property (cost-segregation components, appliances, bonus), which Form 4797 Part III recaptures as ordinary income at up to 37%, is neither modelled nor flagged, though the page links users to cost-segregation and STR-loophole tools.
Basis is reduced only by depreciation 'claimed'; Pub 544 reduces it by depreciation allowed or allowable, so a landlord who skipped depreciation enters 0 and is told there is no recapture.

Capital-gains tax uses one flat user-picked rate with no income stacking, and the recapture rate is min(marginal, 25%) instead of the Schedule D worksheet; a large gain that crosses the 0%/15% or 15%/20% threshold is mis-taxed with no finding, while the page says it applies 'standard capital-gains brackets'.
On a loss the exchange line reads 'the entire -$60,000.00 gain -- and the full $0.00 tax bill -- would be deferred'.

Land value changes no output; depreciableBasis is computed and discarded and depreciation is never checked against purchase - land + improvements, yet vs-doing-it-by-hand.html claims the tool 'keeps land value out of the depreciable basis'.
Loss finding says a 1231 loss is 'subject to the five-year look-back unrecapture rule'; section 1231(c) recharacterizes later net 1231 gains as ordinary, it does not limit this year's loss.
No test covers NIIT on the boot path: computing exchange NIIT on the whole gain instead of the recognized gain survives the suite.

verdict: A small, clean engine whose arithmetic is right for the model it states: five hand recomputations from Pub 544, the Schedule D 1250 worksheet and IRC 1031(b) matched the page in Chromium, 50 tests pass and two of three seeded bugs were caught. It does not reach a CPA's bar: the ordinary-rate override is labelled in dollars and silently reads 0.22 as 0.22% (a 99% understatement of the recapture tax), Section 1245 recapture and the allowed-or-allowable rule are absent and unflagged, the capital-gains rate is one flat pick while the page says it applies brackets, and the README's 'every simplification' finding list misses these. Useful as a back-of-envelope for a straight-line-only residential rental; not to be relied on for a cost-segregated property or a gain that crosses a bracket.
